title: Unbounded Knapsack
directAnswer: Maximize total value within capacity W, but each item may be used any number of times. The recurrence is dp[w] = max over items i of value[i] + dp[w - weight[i]] — taking item i still leaves item i available. Naive recursion is exponential; memoize on remaining capacity or build a 1-D dp[] table iterating weight ASCENDING (so an item can be re-used within the same pass). O(nW).

remember.pattern: Unbounded knapsack — reusable items, 1-D table swept ASCENDING
rules: Each item is reusable **unlimited** times — the take branch recurses on the **same** item set, never shrinking it.
Iterate capacity **ASCENDING** (`1 → W`). That's the exact opposite of 0/1, and it's what lets `dp[w - weight]` already include the item you're adding again.
It's a **max** of value: `dp[w] = max(dp[w], value[i] + dp[w - weight[i]])`.
Anchor `dp[0] = 0` — zero capacity yields zero value — and start every other cell at 0 (taking nothing is always allowed).
Only relax `dp[w]` from a fitting item (`weight[i] <= w`) to avoid a negative index.
whenToUse: Maximize value/score under one capacity with items reusable any number of times
Choosing how many of each denomination/piece to use, repetition allowed
Order of selection doesn't matter, only the multiset of chosen items
Coin Change / Rod Cutting flavored problems (reuse permitted)
antiSignals: Each item usable at most once → 0/1 knapsack, iterate capacity DESCENDING
You want the COUNT of ways to fill, not the max value → counting DP (loop order matters)
Capacity is astronomically large → O(nW) table infeasible, rethink with math/BFS
Fractions allowed → greedy fractional knapsack by ratio, no DP needed
remember.takeaway: Unbounded knapsack is 0/1's twin with one line changed: sweep capacity ascending instead of descending. Ascending lets dp[w - weight] already contain the item you're re-adding, encoding 'use it again'. Coin Change (min count) and Rod Cutting (max price) are unbounded knapsack in disguise — once you see the ascending sweep, you recognize the whole family.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can distinguish reusable-item optimization from the 0/1 case and articulate why the single 1-D loop direction flips from descending to ascending.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Iterating capacity descending out of 0/1 habit (which forbids reuse and undercounts), or shrinking the item set in the take branch as if items were single-use.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the recurrence, then say explicitly: 'this is 0/1 knapsack but the items repeat, so I sweep capacity ascending — dp[w - weight] should already include this item.' Connect it to Coin Change and Rod Cutting.

problemStatement:
You are given `n` item types, where type `i` has a positive `weight[i]` and a positive `value[i]`, and a knapsack of maximum weight capacity `W`.

Maximize the total value of items placed in the knapsack without exceeding `W`. Unlike 0/1 knapsack, you may use each item type an ***unlimited number of times*** (any non-negative count of each).

Return the maximum total value achievable.
constraints: All weights and values are integers
understanding: Fill a knapsack of capacity W to maximize value, where each item type is an inexhaustible supply. The only change from 0/1 knapsack is repetition: after taking an item you may take it again. That single difference flips the space-optimized loop direction and lets the take branch stay on the same item.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I use an item type more than once?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — unlimited copies of each. That's what makes it 'unbounded'. If each were single-use it would be 0/1 knapsack.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is there a limit on how many of one item I can pack?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Only the capacity limits it — you can pack floor(W / weight[i]) copies of item i if that's optimal.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I take a fraction of an item?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, whole items only. Fractions would make it the greedy fractional knapsack problem instead.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if no item fits in W?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The answer is 0 — the empty selection is always valid. The dp array initialized to 0 handles this.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the order I pack items in matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — only the multiset of chosen items affects the value. The DP naturally ignores order.

examples.explanation: Two copies of the weight-4 item (value 50 each) fill capacity 8 for value 100... but weight 3 + weight 5 gives 40 + 70 = 110, the best. Reuse is allowed but not required here.
Two copies of the weight-3 item (8 + 8 = 16) beat three copies of weight-2 (5×3 = 15).
Pack three copies of the weight-3 item (3×3 = 9 ≤ 10) for value 12; a fourth wouldn't fit.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree to run before writing code. Unbounded Knapsack lands on the ascending 1-D table branch.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recursion Over Remaining Capacity
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to establish the reusable-item recurrence, then flag the exponential branching before optimizing.
hints: Think about the NEXT item you place into the remaining capacity. After placing it, what's left to solve?
If you place item i (only when weight[i] ≤ rem), you gain value[i] and still face the SAME item menu with capacity rem - weight[i] — because items are reusable.
best(rem) = max over items i of value[i] + best(rem - weight[i]), with best(0) = 0 and no item fitting → 0.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each call branches into up to n recursive calls and recursion can descend ~W levels (using a weight-1 item), giving exponential nᵂ nodes in the worst case. Stack depth is O(W).
approaches.explanation:
Reason about one placement at a time. To best fill capacity `rem`, try every item `i` that fits, collect `value[i]`, and recursively best-fill the remaining capacity `rem - weight[i]`. Take the maximum over all those choices. The base case is `best(0) = 0`, and if no item fits the result is `0` (pack nothing more).

**The mental shift: place one item, recurse on the same menu.** Don't plan the whole multiset up front. Commit to a single item, reduce the capacity, and solve the identical problem on what remains. The key difference from 0/1: because items repeat, the recursive call faces the *same* full set of items — we do **not** advance an item index or remove anything. That reusability is the entire definition of 'unbounded'.

**Why max of value.** We're choosing the most valuable way to use the remaining room, so we combine the per-item options with `max`. Each option is an alternative, not a companion, so we never sum across items.

**Why the fit guard.** Trying an item heavier than `rem` would index a negative capacity; we only consider items with `weight[i] <= rem`.

**Why we don't ship this.** The same `rem` is recomputed through countless item orderings — exponential overlap on a single state variable. Cache `best(rem)` and the blowup disappears.
approaches.insight: The recurrence depends on exactly one number — the remaining capacity — yet the naive tree resolves `best(rem)` repeatedly via different item orders. One state variable plus heavy overlap is the canonical signal for an O(W·n) DP.

dryRun.intro: best(rem) = max over items of value + best(rem - weight). Items stay reusable, so we recurse on the same menu.

steps.action: item wt2 → 5 + best(4); item wt3 → 8 + best(3)

java.explanation: Base case: no capacity left means no more value can be added — return 0.
Only try items that still fit, so rem - weight[i] never goes negative.

java.line: top = Math.max(top, value[i] + best(weight, value, rem - weight[i]));
java.explanation: Take item i and recurse on the SAME menu — that reuse is what makes it unbounded.

python.explanation: No remaining capacity — base case returns 0.
Guard against a negative remaining capacity.
Recurse over all items, never removing the one just used.

edgeCases.behavior: best(0) returns 0 immediately — nothing can be packed.

pitfalls: Advancing an item index in the recursion — that turns it into 0/1 and forbids reuse.
Forgetting the weight[i] <= rem guard — negative capacity subproblem.
Skipping this approach — interviewers want to hear the recurrence before the table.

approaches.name: Top-Down Memoization on Remaining Capacity
approaches.whenToMention: The fix once you name the overlap — 'cache the best value for each remaining capacity'.
hints: best(rem) returns the same answer every time. Where can you store it so each capacity is solved once?
Add a memo of size W+1 indexed by remaining capacity. Check on entry, fill before returning.
memo[rem] = max over fitting items of value[i] + best(rem - weight[i]); use -1 for 'uncomputed' since 0 is valid.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are W+1 distinct remaining-capacity states. Each does O(n) work scanning items → O(nW) time. The memo plus recursion stack is O(W).
approaches.explanation:
Keep the place-one-item recurrence but cache `best(rem)` so each remaining capacity is solved exactly once. A `memo` array indexed by remaining capacity starts 'uncomputed'; we return the cached value on entry and store the result before returning.

**The mental shift: the answer depends only on the remaining capacity.** Any two paths that arrive at the same `rem` have identical futures, because the item menu never changes (items are unlimited). So the only thing distinguishing a state is how much room is left — caching by `rem` collapses all duplicate explorations into one. The state space is the integers `0..W`, which is why the complexity becomes linear-ish in `W`.

**Why a 1-D memo suffices — unlike 0/1.** In 0/1 knapsack the answer depended on *both* the item index and the capacity (which items remain matters). Here the items never get consumed, so the item index is irrelevant — `rem` alone is the complete state, and a single-dimensional cache is enough.

**Why -1 as sentinel.** 0 is a legitimate best value (nothing fits), so it can't double as 'uncomputed'; initialize the memo to -1.

**A language note.** This top-down version recurses up to `W` deep (with a weight-1 item). For `W = 10⁴` Java handles it, but Python's default recursion limit is about 1000 — deep recursion will raise `RecursionError`. That's the practical reason the bottom-up table (next) is the default in Python.
approaches.insight: Same mechanical DP upgrade as Coin Change: a correct recurrence plus a cache keyed on the only state that matters. The hard part is recognizing that 'remaining capacity' fully determines the future precisely because items are reusable — drop reusability and you'd need the item dimension back.

dryRun.intro: memo[rem] caches the best value for that remaining capacity, filled lazily from W down.

java.explanation: -1 means 'uncomputed' — distinct from the valid best value 0.
Cache hit — return the stored best for this remaining capacity in O(1).

java.line: top = Math.max(top, value[i] + best(weight, value, rem - weight[i], memo));
java.explanation: Try every item; the recursion stays on the full menu, allowing reuse.
Store the resolved best before returning so this capacity is never recomputed.

python.explanation: Caches best by its single argument rem — a clean 1-D top-down memo.
Reuse permitted: the recursive call sees all items again. Caution: depth up to W can exceed Python's ~1000 recursion limit.

pitfalls: Using 0 as 'uncomputed' — collides with the valid answer 0; use -1.
Indexing the memo at W instead of W+1 entries — capacities 0..W need W+1 slots.
Deep recursion in Python (rem up to W) can blow the ~1000 recursion limit — prefer tabulation for large W.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up — 1-D dp[] Table, Capacity ASCENDING (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'fill dp[0..W] ascending; reuse is what the ascending sweep gives you for free'.
hints: Compute the best value for capacity 1, then 2, ... up to W, reusing earlier answers.
dp[w] = best value within capacity w. dp[0] = 0; for each w try every fitting item: dp[w] = max(dp[w], value[i] + dp[w - weight[i]]).
Sweep w ASCENDING. Because dp[w - weight] is already finalized AND may itself include item i, the same item gets reused automatically — the opposite of 0/1's descending sweep.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The outer loop runs W times, the inner loop scans n items → O(nW) time. A single dp array of size W+1 → O(W) space, no recursion stack.
approaches.explanation:
Build the answers bottom-up. `dp[w]` is the maximum value that fits in capacity `w`. Anchor `dp[0] = 0`, then for each capacity `w` from `1` to `W`, try every item that fits and relax `dp[w] = max(dp[w], value[i] + dp[w - weight[i]])`. The answer is `dp[W]`.

**The mental shift: solve every smaller capacity first.** Because `dp[w]` only looks *down* to `dp[w - weight]` for positive weights, processing capacities in increasing order guarantees every dependency is final when you reach it. No recursion, no stack — one clean sweep.

**Why ASCENDING is the whole trick.** This is the mirror image of 0/1 knapsack. When we relax `dp[w]` using `dp[w - weight[i]]`, that smaller cell has *already been updated in this same pass* and may itself include item `i`. So adding item `i` again on top of it means we've used item `i` multiple times — exactly the reuse we want. In 0/1 we iterated descending precisely to *prevent* this; here we iterate ascending to *enable* it. One loop direction, two completely different problems.

**Why one shared array works without an item dimension.** Since items are reusable, the item index is not part of the state — only the capacity is. A single `dp[w]` over capacities, swept ascending while looping items inside, captures every multiset. (Looping capacities outer and items inner, or items outer and capacities inner, both work for the max-value version because order of items doesn't matter here.)

**Why dp[0] = 0 anchors everything.** Every reachable capacity's value is built from `dp[0]` through a chain of item additions. Leave `dp[0]` unset and no capacity could be relaxed.
approaches.insight: Unbounded knapsack is the parent of Coin Change (min count) and Rod Cutting (max price): all three are 'reusable items, fill a target' DPs distinguished only by the objective. The ascending sweep is the signature — see it and you know reuse is allowed. Flip to descending and you've silently switched to 0/1.

dryRun.intro: dp[w] = best value within capacity w. Sweep w ascending; dp[w - weight] may already include the item, enabling reuse.

java.explanation: dp[w] = best value within capacity w; defaults to 0, which is also the dp[0] anchor.
ASCENDING capacities — dp[w - weight] is already final and may include this item, enabling reuse.
Only relax with items that fit, so w - weight[i] is non-negative.
Take item i on top of the best fill of the remaining capacity. The whole DP in one line.

python.explanation: All capacities start at 0; index 0 is the base case (zero value).
Ascending sweep — the single line that distinguishes unbounded from 0/1 knapsack.
dp[w - weight] can already contain item i, so item i is reused freely.

diagrams.title: Filling dp[] left to right (ascending)
diagrams.caption: dp[w] = best value within capacity w for weight=[2,3], value=[5,8]. Ascending order lets items repeat.

edgeCases.behavior: Outer loop never runs; dp[0] = 0 returned — empty knapsack.
dp[w] = w × value, packing W copies of the unit item.
Inner guard always fails; dp stays 0 → answer 0.

pitfalls: Iterating capacity DESCENDING out of 0/1 habit — forbids reuse and undercounts the value.
Forgetting the weight[i] <= w guard — negative index into dp.
Confusing this with the COUNT-of-ways variant, where the item/capacity loop nesting changes the meaning.

commonMistakes: Iterating capacity descending (0/1 style), which blocks item reuse and gives the wrong, smaller value.
Removing/advancing the item in the take branch as if items were single-use.
Treating 0 as 'uncomputed' in the memo when 0 is a valid best value.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Descending sweep kills reuse
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Descending order keeps dp[w - weight] at its pre-item value, which is exactly 0/1 behavior. For unbounded you WANT dp[w - weight] to already include the item, so you must sweep ascending.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Advancing the item index in recursion
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Recursing on i+1 (or shrinking the item list) forbids reusing an item — that's the 0/1 recurrence. Unbounded must recurse on the SAME item set.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sentinel collides with a valid 0
commonMistakesDetailed.why: 0 is a legitimate best value (nothing fits), so it can't also mean 'uncomputed'. Initialize the memo to -1.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int[] memo = new int[W + 1]; // all 0
if (memo[rem] != 0) return memo[rem];

followupVariations.title: Coin Change
followupVariations.hint: Unbounded knapsack minimizing the COUNT of items to hit an exact target — swap max-value for min-count.

followupVariations.title: Coin Change II
followupVariations.hint: Count the NUMBER OF ways to fill the target with reusable coins — loop coins outer to avoid counting permutations.

followupVariations.title: Rod Cutting
followupVariations.hint: Maximize price by cutting a rod — unbounded knapsack where a length-i piece is a reusable 'item' of weight i and value price[i].

followupVariations.title: Combination Sum IV
followupVariations.hint: Count ordered sequences (permutations) summing to target — capacity outer, items inner.

patternNote: Canonical unbounded knapsack — reusable-item value maximization. Recognize it whenever you fill one capacity to optimize value with each item type available unlimited times. Identical skeleton to Coin Change (min count) and Rod Cutting (max price); the ascending capacity sweep is what distinguishes it from 0/1 knapsack.
